questions.question: Identify the synonym of 'Fickle':
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **Option 2 i.e. Unpredictable**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The word **"Fickle"** means someone or something that changes frequently or unpredictably, especially in terms of loyalty or preferences. (चंचल, अस्थिर)
 
 
• **Example:** The weather in this region is fickle; it can be sunny one moment and raining the next.
 
 
• **"Unpredictable"** refers to something that cannot be anticipated or foreseen, aligning perfectly with the meaning of "fickle". (अप्रत्याशित)
 
 
• **Example:** His unpredictable behavior makes it hard to rely on him during critical situations.
 
 
• Hence, we can conclude that the synonym of **'Fickle' **is **'Unpredictable'**.

Therefore, the correct answer is: **Option 2 i.e. Unpredictable**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

Here are the other options explained along with their Hindi meanings and example sentences:

 
• **Constant** (स्थिर): Something that remains the same over time and does not change.
 
 
• **Example:** She has been a constant source of support for me during tough times.
 
 
 
• **Reliable** (विश्वसनीय): Something or someone that can be depended upon and trusted.
 
 
• **Example:** This car is reliable and has never broken down in the last five years.
 
 
 
• **Stable** (स्थिर): Something that is firmly established and unlikely to change or fluctuate.
 
 
• **Example:** The political situation in the country has become stable after years of turmoil.

questions.question:
Fill in the blank with the most appropriate adverb.

He completed the task ______ than anyone expected.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**faster**'.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The word **"faster"** is the comparative degree of the adverb **"fast."**
 
• When comparing two actions or situations, and the word **"than"** is present in the sentence, the comparative form of the modifier must be used.
 
• For short, one-syllable adverbs like "fast," the comparative is formed by adding the suffix **"-er."**

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

**Complete Sentence:** *"He completed the task **faster**__ than anyone expected."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: "fast"** is the positive degree. It is used for simple descriptions without comparison (e.g., "He ran fast").
 
• **Option 3: "fastest"** is the superlative degree, used when comparing one person or thing to a group of three or more.
 
• **Option 4: "most fast"** is grammatically incorrect. Adverbs that take "-er" for comparison do not use "more" or "most."

questions.question:
Fill in the blank with most appropriate option:

This book is ___ than the one I read last week.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**more interesting**'.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The word **"more interesting"** is the comparative degree of the adjective **"interesting."**
 
• When comparing two things (this book and the one from last week) and using the word **"than,"** the comparative degree is required.
 
• For adjectives with three or more syllables (like in-ter-est-ing), the comparative form is created by adding the word **"more"** before the adjective.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

**Complete Sentence:** *"This book is **more interesting**__ than the one I read last week."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: "interesting"** is the positive degree, used for a simple description of one thing without comparison.
 
• **Option 2: "interest"** is a noun or a verb, not an adjective that can fit this comparative structure.
 
• **Option 4: "most interesting"** is the superlative degree, used when comparing one thing to a group of three or more (e.g., "This is the most interesting book in the library").

questions.question:
Fill in the blank with most appropriate option:

The manager wants the report ___ by tomorrow morning.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**submitted**'.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The sentence follows the grammatical structure: **Subject + Verb (want/need/get) + Object + Past Participle**.
 
• This structure is used when we want to say that we would like something to be done by someone else. The object (the report) receives the action.
 
• The **past participle** ("**submitted**") acts as an object complement, describing the required state of the report.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

**Complete Sentence:** *"The manager wants the report **submitted**__ by tomorrow morning."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: "submit"** is the base form of the verb. While you could say "The manager wants him **to submit** the report," you cannot use the base form directly after the object "report."
 
• **Option 2: "submitting"** is the present participle. Using it here would imply the report is the one performing the action of submitting, which is incorrect.
 
• **Option 4: "submits"** is the third-person singular present form. It cannot function as a complement to the object in this sentence structure.

questions.question:

You should not look ___ upon people who have less than you.
questions.solution:

__
 
• The sentence requires a **phrasal verb** that means to regard someone as inferior or to think you are better than them.
 
• The phrasal verb **"look down upon"** (or "look down on") perfectly fits this context, especially when referring to social status or wealth.
 
• This is a common idiomatic expression used to give moral advice about treating everyone with respect.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

**Complete Sentence:** *"You should not look **down**__ upon people who have less than you."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 2: "look in"** means to pay a short visit to someone (e.g., "I'll look in on my neighbor later").
 
• **Option 3: "look over"** means to examine or inspect something quickly (e.g., "Look over your notes before the exam").
 
• **Option 4: "look forward"** is usually used as part of the phrase "look forward to," meaning to await something with excitement.

questions.question:
Fill in the blank with most appropriate option:

The professor spoke so ___ that many students lost interest.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**monotonously**'.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The sentence requires a word to modify the verb **"spoke."** Words that describe how an action is performed are **adverbs**.
 
• **"Monotonously"** is the adverb form of the word, meaning to speak in a dull, unvarying tone.
 
• The sentence follows the **"so + adverb + that"** structure, which is used to show cause and effect (the boring speech caused the students to lose interest).

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

**Complete Sentence:** *"The professor spoke so **monotonously**__ that many students lost interest."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: "monotony"** is a **noun** referring to the state of being tedious or repetitive (e.g., "The monotony of the job was tiring").
 
• **Option 2: "monotonous"** is an **adjective**. It describes a noun, not a verb (e.g., "He has a monotonous voice").
 
• **Option 4: "monotonic"** is also an **adjective**, often used in technical, mathematical, or phonological contexts to describe a sequence that stays the same.

questions.question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:

The baby sleep (1) / quietly through (2) / the loud thunderstorm (3) / which amazed us(4).
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The primary error in the sentence is a lack of **subject-verb agreement** and **tense consistency** in part (1).
 
• The subject "**The baby**" is a singular noun. In the simple present tense, the verb should be "**sleeps**."
 
• However, because the second half of the sentence uses the past tense ("**amazed**"), the first part should also be in the past tense to maintain consistency.
 
• The past tense of the irregular verb "sleep" is "**slept**."
 
• Therefore, "The baby sleep" is grammatically incorrect.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"The baby **slept** quietly through the loud thunderstorm which amazed us."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **(2): "quietly through"** – This part is correct. The adverb "quietly" properly modifies the verb, and "through" is the correct preposition indicating the duration of the storm.
 
• **(3): "the loud thunderstorm"** – This is a standard noun phrase acting as the object of the preposition and is grammatically correct.
 
• **(4): "which amazed us."** – This is a relative clause providing extra information about the preceding situation. The use of the past tense "amazed" is what dictates the need for the past tense earlier in the sentence.

questions.question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:

The teacher asked the students (1) / to write neatly (2) / and answer (3) / each questions carefully(4).
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 4**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The error is located in part (4) of the sentence due to incorrect **noun-determiner agreement**.
 
• The word "**each**" is a distributive determiner that must always be followed by a **singular countable noun**.
 
• In this sentence, "**questions**" is a plural noun, which is grammatically incompatible with "each." It should be changed to the singular form "**question**."
 
• Thus, the phrase should correctly read: "**each question carefully**."

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 4**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"The teacher asked the students to write neatly and answer **each question** carefully."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **(1): "The teacher asked the students"** – This part is grammatically correct, establishing the subject and the indirect object.
 
• **(2): "to write neatly"** – This is a correct use of the infinitive ("to write") followed by an adverb ("neatly") to describe the manner of writing.
 
• **(3): "and answer"** – This maintains parallel structure with "to write." The "to" is understood/carried over to the second verb ("to [write... and] answer").

questions.question:
Arrange the sentences to create a relatable classroom scenario:
(1) The teacher smiled, knowing well that the answer was written on the student's hand.
(2) Everyone turned silent as the teacher asked the unexpected question.
(3) Rahul stood up slowly, avoiding eye contact.
(4) "Rahul, can you answer that?" the teacher asked.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 4**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
 
• The sentences are designed to create a relatable classroom scenario, with a logical flow of actions and reactions. 
 
• **Sentence 2** comes first because it sets the stage with silence in the classroom as the teacher asks an unexpected question: 
 
 
• "Everyone turned silent as the teacher asked the unexpected question." 
 
 
 
• **Sentence 4** follows as the teacher directs the question to Rahul, creating a moment of tension: 
 
 
• "‘Rahul, can you answer that?’ the teacher asked." 
 
 
 
• **Sentence 3** comes next as Rahul reacts to the teacher’s question, showing hesitation and avoiding eye contact: 
 
 
• "Rahul stood up slowly, avoiding eye contact." 
 
 
 
• **Sentence 1** concludes the scenario with the teacher’s knowing smile, implying awareness of the situation:

questions.question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:

She adopted a orphan (1) / and raised him (2) / as her own child (3) / with love (4).
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The error is found in part (1) of the sentence and concerns the incorrect use of the **indefinite article**.
 
• The rule for indefinite articles is to use "**a**" before words beginning with a consonant sound and "**an**" before words beginning with a **vowel sound**.
 
• The word "**orphan**" starts with the vowel sound /ɔː/, which requires the article "**an**" instead of "a."
 
• Therefore, the phrase "a orphan" must be corrected to "**an orphan**."

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"She adopted **an orphan** and raised him as her own child with love."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **(2): "and raised him"** – This part is correct. "Raised" is the past tense of "raise," meaning to bring up a child.
 
• **(3): "as her own child"** – This phrase is grammatically correct and uses "as" to show the role or capacity in which the person was raised.
 
• **(4): "with love."** – This is a prepositional phrase acting as an adverb of manner, which is used correctly here.

questions.question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:

This book is (1) / gooder than (2) / the one we read (3) / last month(4).
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The error is found in part (2) of the sentence and involves the incorrect formation of a **comparative adjective**.
 
• The adjective "**good**" is irregular. It does not follow the standard rule of adding "-er" to form its comparative degree.
 
• The correct comparative form of "good" is "**better**," and the superlative form is "**best**."
 
• Therefore, "gooder" is grammatically incorrect and must be replaced with "**better**."

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"This book is **better than** the one we read last month."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **(1): "This book is"** – This part is correct; it identifies the singular subject and the appropriate linking verb.
 
• **(3): "the one we read"** – This is a correct way to refer back to a previously mentioned noun ("book"). The verb "read" is in the past tense here (pronounced like "red").
 
• **(4): "last month."** – This is a standard adverbial phrase of time and is grammatically correct.

questions.question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:

They enjoyed (1) / the sceneries (2) / during their trip (3) / to the mountains(4).
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The error is in part (2) of the sentence and relates to the use of **uncountable nouns**.
 
• The word "**scenery**" is an uncountable (mass) noun in English. It refers to the general appearance of a place and does not have a plural form.
 
• Using "sceneries" is grammatically incorrect. Even when referring to multiple beautiful views, we still use the singular form "**scenery**."
 
• Other examples of such nouns include *furniture, advice, information,* and *poetry*.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"They enjoyed the **scenery** during their trip to the mountains."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **(1): "They enjoyed"** – This part is correct; it uses the simple past tense to describe a completed action in the past.
 
• **(3): "during their trip"** – This is a correct prepositional phrase indicating the time or occasion of the action.
 
• **(4): "to the mountains."** – This is a standard prepositional phrase indicating the destination or location, which is grammatically correct.
